chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Fazalat ibn Ayoub, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Ismail ibn Ja'far, who said:

Two men disputed before Dawud (peace be upon him) regarding a cow. So this one came with a proof that it belonged to him, and this one came with a proof that it belonged to him. He said: So Dawud (peace be upon him) entered the Mihrab (prayer niche) and said: 'O Lord, it has become difficult for me to judge between these two, so You be the One who judges.' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: 'Exit and take the cow from the one in whose hand it is, then give it to the other, and strike his neck.'

He (the narrator) said: So the Children of Israel made a commotion about that, and they said: 'This one came with a proof, and this one came with a proof, and it would have been more rightful to give it to the one in whose hand it was.' But he took it from him, struck his neck, and gave it to this one.

He (the narrator) said: So Dawud entered the Mihrab and said: 'O Lord, the Children of Israel have made a commotion regarding what You judged with.' So his Lord revealed to him: 'The one in whose hand the cow was met the father of the other one, so he killed him and took the cow from him. So when they come to you with the like of this, judge between them with what you see, and do not ask Me to judge until the Reckoning.'

key_terms.الْمِحْرَابُ: Prayer niche or place of worship/judgment
key_terms.دَاوُدُ: Prophet Dawud (David), peace be upon him

ai.seo_question: How did Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) resolve a dispute over a cow with divine guidance?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the transition from direct divine revelation (*wahy*) in judicial matters to human reasoning (*ijtihad*) in Islamic jurisprudence. While Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) initially received specific divine instruction to resolve the dispute over the cow, God clarified that for future cases, he should rely on his own judgment based on available evidence, marking a shift toward the principle of *hukm al-qadi* (the judge's ruling). This narrative underscores the Shia scholarly view that while prophets possessed infallible knowledge, the mechanism for resolving legal disputes among the community evolved to empower human intellect within divine parameters.
